name: keras
title: Keras: A Multi-Backend Deep Learning Library for AI
answer: Keras is an open-source Python deep learning library, now at version 3, that runs on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO. It provides high-level building blocks for neural networks, including layers, models, optimizers, and training loops, and is used for tasks from image classification to text generation. The key thing to know is that Keras 3 lets you write one codebase and switch backends, so you can prototype quickly and then deploy with the performance characteristics you need.

sections.body: Keras is an open-source deep learning library for Python, created by François Chollet and now maintained by the Keras team. It sits at the high-level API layer of the AI stack, offering a user-friendly interface for building and training neural networks. Since Keras 3.0, it is multi-backend, meaning it can run on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO for inference. It provides over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, and training loops. The library is licensed under Apache-2.0 and has a large community, with over 64,000 stars on GitHub and adoption by more than 2.5 million developers.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Keras is used for the full range of deep learning jobs: training, evaluation, inference, data preprocessing, and model serving. It excels in rapid prototyping and research, thanks to its simple, consistent APIs like Sequential, Functional, and subclassing. It is strong for standard architectures such as convolutional networks for image classification, transformers for text, and autoencoders. With Keras 3, it is also a cross-framework language for custom components that work across backends. It is particularly well-suited for developers who want to experiment quickly and then scale to production, as it supports distributed training and can export models to TensorFlow SavedModel or PyTorch. However, for highly specialized low-level control, other frameworks may be preferred.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed to be approachable, with a gentle learning curve compared to lower-level frameworks. Prerequisites include basic Python programming and a understanding of fundamental machine learning concepts such as layers, loss functions, and optimizers. Some mathematics, like linear algebra and calculus, helps for custom components, but the official guides start with simple examples like MNIST classification. The official website offers extensive documentation, guides, and examples, including a getting started section, functional API guide, and training with built-in methods. A beginner can follow along and build models within hours, though mastering advanced features like custom training loops or multi-backend distribution may require more systems knowledge.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: Keras has a rich ecosystem. It integrates with KerasHub for pretrained models and components, and supports data loading from NumPy arrays, tf.data.Dataset, PyTorch DataLoader, and Pandas dataframes. The official site provides comprehensive documentation, API references, and a large collection of examples, from image classification to text generation with GPT. The community is active, with contributions on GitHub and discussions on forums. Keras 3's multi-backend design means it works with the JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch ecosystems, and custom layers using keras.ops are portable across backends. The site also mentions that Keras powers systems like Waymo's self-driving fleet and YouTube's recommendation engine, indicating strong industry trust.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both quick experiments and production deployment. Its high-level APIs like Sequential and Functional make prototyping fast, with built-in training loops that handle batching, validation, and metrics. For production, Keras 3 allows you to switch backends to optimize performance: JAX typically delivers the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU, and CPU, though non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU. The library also supports model parallelism and data parallelism through the keras.distribution API, currently implemented for JAX. The cost is that using the high-level API may abstract away some low-level control, but you can drop down to custom layers and training loops when needed, and the same code can run across backends.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: Keras is widely adopted in industry and academia. The official site states it has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine. It is a current standard, not a legacy choice, especially with Keras 3's multi-backend support. For someone choosing it for work, Keras skills are valuable for roles in machine learning engineering, data science, and AI research, as it is used for rapid prototyping and production. However, the facts do not specify exact job market data or salary trends, so those considering careers should research current demand. The library's integration with TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch means it complements rather than replaces those frameworks.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is typically used with Python and sits alongside lower-level frameworks like TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch. In a polyglot pattern, Keras acts as the high-level API that can run on any of these backends, allowing developers to write one codebase and switch backends for performance or deployment needs. It is often used with TensorFlow as tf.keras, but Keras 3 makes it backend-agnostic. It also integrates with KerasHub for pretrained models and supports data pipelines from NumPy, Pandas, tf.data, and PyTorch DataLoader. This makes Keras a central piece in a multi-framework workflow, where custom components written with keras.ops can be shared across JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Keras is not ideal for every scenario. Its high-level abstractions can limit fine-grained control over computations, which may be necessary for novel research or highly optimized systems. The distribution API is currently only implemented for the JAX backend, with TensorFlow and PyTorch support coming soon, so distributed training on those backends may be less mature. The official site does not specify performance benchmarks for all model types, and results vary. Also, while Keras 3 supports OpenVINO for inference, it is not a training backend. The site does not detail memory management or edge deployment specifics, so those considering embedded or mobile use should investigate further. Finally, the facts do not cover community size beyond GitHub stars, so the breadth of third-party tutorials and support is not fully quantified.
